idiom_name: memoized reader: @value ||= build, or a defined? guard
implementation_notes: Ruby defers construction inside an ordinary reader method: `@image ||= Image.load(@path)` runs the expensive construction on the first call and returns the instance variable afterwards, and `return @image if defined?(@image)` is the correct guard when the result itself can be false or nil. The operator is falsy-based rather than defined?-based, so a legitimately nil or false result re-runs the construction on every call - the best-known Ruby memoization trap. Writing the explicit stand-in class is only worth it when several methods must share one guard, when the cached value needs invalidation, or when the object must satisfy an interface rather than being read through a reader.
pitfalls: `||=` memoization silently re-runs the construction whenever the computed value is false or nil; use defined? (or a separate built? flag) when those are valid results.
Instance-variable memoization is not thread-safe: on JRuby or TruffleRuby two threads can both build, and even on MRI the GVL does not protect an initializer that blocks on IO.
Memoization assumes the inputs never change; assigning @path later leaves the stale real object cached, and there is no built-in invalidation.
